threads.topic: A year-end report with no year-end CFR

entries.q: The year-end report's balance-sheet table is the estimate from the 2025/26 strategy, not the outturn. Actual debt of £706.282m came in £132.5m below that forecast. What was the actual capital financing requirement at 31 March 2026, and what is the resulting under-borrowing?
entries.why: Under-borrowing is the figure that says how much has been spent and not yet financed. The strategy put it at £296.344m; debt landed far below forecast, so the real number is bigger and it is not in the report. The same report also gives external debt as both £706.282m and £715.97m.

threads.topic: HRA financing costs nearly doubling by 2030/31

entries.q: HRA financing costs are budgeted to rise from 11.00% of gross income to 18.33% by 2030/31, with interest payable going from £6.381m to £13.605m. What rate does that assume on new HRA borrowing, and what happens to the business plan if it is a point higher?
entries.why: The General Fund ratio is comfortable and the report says so. The HRA ratio is set to grow by two thirds over five years and the report does not comment on it at all.

entries.q: The loans to the SSDC Opium Power joint venture are carried at a fair value of £29.800m against £42.478m invested, and the report says this is subject to an ongoing corporate assessment. What is the assessment expected to conclude, and is MRP still being charged on the full principal?
entries.why: Loan repayments were the mechanism funding MRP on this investment. If the loans are worth less than the borrowing behind them, the shortfall falls on the General Fund and the report flags the possibility without sizing it.

threads.topic: Two fifths of the debt due within a year

entries.q: 39.4% of borrowing matures within twelve months, kept deliberately short against expected property receipts and a £95m DSG settlement due in 2026/27. If either slips, what does refinancing that £278m cost at today's rates rather than the 4.07% the book currently averages?
entries.why: Short borrowing is the cheap and correct answer when you know cash is coming. It is the expensive one if the cash is late, and both sources here depend on someone else's timetable.

summary.text:
A large unitary running down a commercial property portfolio it inherited, and using the proceeds to hold its debt flat. External borrowing closed 2025/26 at £706.282m, down £13.096m on the year, at an average 4.07% — cheaper than the 4.17% it started at, because £173.096m matured and only £160.000m was taken to replace it. The General Fund affordability ratio is 6.97%, and the report is right to point out that CIPFA's recommended maximum is 10%. On the General Fund, this is a well-run book.

The Housing Revenue Account is the other story. Financing costs there take 11.00% of gross rental income today and the council's own budget takes that to 13.79% next year, 16.72% the year after, and 18.33% by 2030/31 — a near doubling in five years, driven by HRA interest payable rising from £6.381m to £13.605m while gross income grows only from £58.019m to £74.223m. It is set out plainly in the report and not commented on.

The year-end report does not state a year-end CFR. Its balance-sheet table is the forecast from the strategy written a year earlier, which put the borrowing need at £1,135.076m and under-borrowing at £296.344m. Actual debt came in £132.5m below that same forecast, because property sales and repayments went further than planned. So the true under-borrowing at 31 March is materially larger than £296m, and a member cannot work out how much larger from the paper in front of them. The report also gives external debt twice — £706.282m in the portfolio table and £715.97m against the authorised limit — without reconciling them.

The commercial portfolio is being sold, and the numbers are worth stating plainly. £301.226m was originally invested. It was valued at £222.411m by March 2024, £111.106m by March 2025, and £82.272m still stands at 31 March 2026 after £33.308m of sales during the year — those sales at a £4.715m net gain on book value, which is the encouraging part. Alongside it sits a battery-storage joint venture inherited from South Somerset: £42.478m invested, fair value now £29.800m, and the report notes that value is subject to an ongoing corporate assessment.

Two structural points. 39.4% of the debt matures within twelve months — the largest bucket in the book, against a 50% ceiling — because borrowing was deliberately kept short to match expected property receipts and a £95m Dedicated Schools Grant settlement due from government in 2026/27. That is a coherent plan that depends on both arriving. And £103.000m of the £131.150m investment book sits in pooled funds carried at cost, whose market value is £94.211m — an £8.8m unrealised shortfall held off the revenue account by a statutory override that expires in March 2029.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 2025/26 treasury outturn. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Some context on our side first. We hold 71 PWLB loans for Somerset, at a balance today of £492.3m against the £512.8m of PWLB in your 31 March position — the two aren't meant to tie, because ours is four months later and picks up what has amortised and matured since.

The General Fund book reads well and we'd say so. External borrowing closed at £706.282m, down £13.096m, at an average 4.07% against 4.17% a year earlier, because £173.096m matured and only £160.000m was drawn to replace it. Financing costs are 6.97% of the General Fund net revenue stream and your report is right to note CIPFA's recommended maximum of 10%.

The Housing Revenue Account is the part we'd draw attention to, and only because your own report sets it out and then leaves it there. Financing costs take 11.00% of gross rental income now, and your own budget takes that to 13.79% next year, 16.72% the year after and 18.33% by 2030/31 — HRA interest payable going from £6.381m to £13.605m while gross income moves only from £58.019m to £74.223m. A near doubling of the ratio in five years is the kind of thing that is much easier to discuss while it is still a forecast. We have no recommendation about it; we simply notice that it is the most significant number in the report and it is not commented on.

Second, and this is genuinely a question rather than an observation: the year-end report doesn't state a year-end CFR. The balance sheet table carries the forecast from the strategy written a year earlier — £1,135.076m of borrowing need and £296.344m of under-borrowing. But actual debt came in about £132.5m below that same forecast, because property sales and repayments went further than planned, so the real under-borrowing at 31 March must be materially larger than £296m. We haven't put a number on it and won't, because you have the figure and we don't. It matters mainly because the liability benchmark and everything downstream of it keys off the actual.

Third, the near end. 39.4% of the book matures inside twelve months, against a 50% ceiling and a 15% floor — comfortably the largest bucket you have. One-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26 and two-year at 5.06%, and July's sector borrowing was thin: £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. When nearly two-fifths of a £706m book turns over annually, the depth of the market on the day matters as much as the rate. That's at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Two smaller things. Your £93.000m of LOBOs sat unchanged all year with no call exercised — which is notable, because we've picked up five calls elsewhere in a few months (Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York and Barnet), all of them lenders testing options now that PWLB rates have risen to meet them. That's a cross-council pattern no single council can see from its own papers, and yours is the largest untested LOBO book we hold.

And on pricing: 41 of your PWLB loans sit below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve today, against 29 above, netting to roughly £63.4m of discount. Most of it is in two loans — £20m at 1.89% to 2071 and £10m at 1.64% to 2070. At the other end, three legacy loans at 8.38%, 7.38% and 6.63% maturing 2056 and 2057 carry about £0.99m of premium on just £4m of principal. We're not suggesting anything follows: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Somerset. HRA treasury & self-financing and HRA Liability Benchmark: two-pool go directly to the ratio above — the two-pool question is exactly what an 18.33% forecast turns on. LOBO loans (legacy) for the £93m. And The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), which is written for members. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
